dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment

evidence.note: Solid environment orientation: checks Python version, reads start.sh/requirements.txt/app skeleton, and verifies SQLite JSON1 support before building on it.
Error envelope, cards.py test-PAN set, and error codes written directly from memory ('Stripe's published test PAN set') with no external reference, doc fetch, or SDK check.

Correctly recalls hard-part semantics — decline returns PI with last_payment_error at HTTP 402, capturing a succeeded PI = 400 unexpected_state, decline error-body idempotency replay — but all confirmed only via curl against its own service, not real Stripe/SDK.

No WebFetch, no `import stripe`, no api_base/SDK round-trip anywhere; the externally-defined contract is reconstructed purely from the model's recall and never grounded in the actual API/SDK behavior the fidelity is graded against.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error {type,code,...} mapping, list envelope, test-PAN set — and even recalls the hard-part semantics (idempotency scope, decline replay, state-machine 400s) accurately, which is clearly above anchor 3. But every bit of contract knowledge comes from memory: there is zero grounding in real SDK round-trips or Stripe docs, no confirmation of how the SDK sets api_base/auth, and all 'verification' is self-referential curl against its own service. That absence of external grounding and probing keeps it well below anchors 8-10, landing it at 5.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps

evidence.note: Recognized the surface as large and laid a layered build order: core infra (incl. idempotency.py, webhooks.py, billing.py) before route modules — the three traps got dedicated first-class modules rather than being buried in CRUD.
Construction was breadth-first: all core modules then every route in sequence, with no risk-front-loading and no incremental boot checkpoints in the build order.
First boot and health verification came only AFTER the entire surface was written — no early bootable/auth'd skeleton verified while budget remained.

During testing, treated the three traps as distinct workstreams each with an explicit done-condition: idempotency replay returns same IDs, decline returns 402, capturing succeeded PI returns 400 unexpected_state, decline replay returns identical 402 body.
Closed with a coverage tally and start.sh boot check, mapping verification back onto the resource list — done-conditions present but as a reactive checklist, not a pre-declared milestone hierarchy.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly cleared the level-5 bar: a layered order (infra→routes→wire→boot→test) with the three traps recognized as distinct workstreams and given dedicated modules plus explicit verification done-conditions (402 / 400 unexpected_state / same-ID replay). It edges above 5 because the trap subsystems were carved out as first-class modules and checked with concrete expected outcomes rather than a flat 'returns 200' checklist. But it falls short of 8/10 because there was no early bootable skeleton verified while budget remained (it built the whole surface before the first boot), construction was breadth-first with no risk-front-loading or explicit dependency ordering, and the 'plan' was regenerated reactively per step rather than maintained as a milestone hierarchy — placing it at a 6.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks

evidence.note: Booted service, verified health, then targeted curl checks: idempotency replay returns same IDs (48), same-key-different-body → 400 idempotency_error (49), decline card → 402 with verbose HTTP-status confirmation (50-53). Beyond happy-path.
Verified illegal state transitions: capturing a succeeded PI → 400 payment_intent_unexpected_state, cancel of succeeded PI → 400. Directly exercises the state-machine trap.

Verified idempotency replay of a cached decline/error body — both requests return HTTP 402 with identical body — after rewriting the confirm route; re-run after a fix, a hallmark of deliberate verification.
Verified auth 401 (no/bad key), revoked key 401, restricted-key permission 403, and events filtering — broad error/HTTP-code coverage.

Tested GET charge/invoice/events-deliveries and start.sh boot. But events/deliveries returned empty and webhook 5xx retry/backoff + re-signing were never actively exercised; concurrency serialization untested; the stripe SDK itself was never used — all checks were raw curl.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well past anchor 5: it deliberately verified the idempotency traps (replay with same IDs, cached error-body replay, same-key-different-body 400) and the full state-machine illegal transitions (capture/cancel of succeeded → 400), plus error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, and 401/403, re-running checks after fixes. That matches most of anchor 8's targeted trap verification. However it never verified through the actual stripe SDK against api_base (anchor 8's explicit requirement), and left the webhook 5xx retry/backoff, re-signing, and concurrent same-key serialization traps unverified — so it falls short of a full 8, landing at 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface

evidence.note: During the build phase, every step's Plan/Analysis enumerates completed route files and the exact remaining ones (charges, refunds, products, prices, subscriptions, invoices, events, webhook_endpoints, restricted_keys), showing continuous accounting against the full route table.

Maintains a persistent, growing 'bugs identified' list (confirm idempotency, decline caching hash mismatch, lock release, billing circular import) alongside an untested-endpoints list, reallocating between building, testing and fixing without dropping items.

Explicitly restates full coverage status ('health, customers... through webhook endpoints') and enumerates the remaining trap tests (decline idempotency replay, revoked key 401, permission 403), then executes each — distinguishing implemented from verified.
Final explicit numbered checklist with checkmarks across all 12+ resource families plus idempotency/state-machine/webhook traps before submitting; confirms nothing major was silently skipped.

Notices side-effects that could distort the picture (DB reset wiped charges; deliveries empty because no endpoint existed at event time) and recreates data to re-verify — accurate state tracking rather than false 'done'.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively maintained coverage against the entire route table and trap set from start to finish, consistently distinguishing done-from-remaining and implemented-from-verified, with an explicit final checklist — matching the level-8 anchor. It did not reach 10 because it never explicitly named thrashing/time-boxed a stuck behavior and left webhook retry/backoff flagged-but-unverified rather than closing that loop, so continuous accounting fell just short of the top anchor.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures

evidence.note: Idempotency replay failed with internal error; agent diagnosed the true cause (headers double-parsed via json.loads on an already-parsed dict) and fixed the underlying inconsistency rather than patching the call site.

Recognized the confirm route's idempotency was structurally inconsistent with central check_idempotency (json.dumps(data) vs raw body, no lock release, no key check) and rewrote it to route through the central mechanism — propagating the idempotency model across endpoints, not just fixing one symptom.

Fixed restricted-key auth lookup via json_extract (step 70), then still hit a 500 at step 78; traced it to a table-schema mismatch and realigned restricted_keys to the standard (id,object,data,created) pattern — a structural fix, though it addressed the lookup symptom before the deeper schema model.

On realizing no routes actually enforced restricted-key permissions, added permission checks across routes (master-only for webhook/restricted-key management, scoped checks on customers) and re-verified 403/401 behavior — propagating a fix across the surface.
After the confirm-route rewrite, re-ran the decline-replay test and confirmed identical 402 bodies, showing corrections were verified rather than assumed, while earlier-verified flows were preserved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently diagnosed root causes rather than tweaking surface fields, and in the most consequential cases (confirm-route idempotency rewrite, restricted_keys schema realignment, permission enforcement) it updated its model and propagated fixes across related code while re-verifying — matching much of the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because most divergences were against its own implementation rather than genuine external-contract surprises, and one instance (restricted keys) shows it patching the auth-lookup symptom before uncovering the deeper schema mismatch. This places it solidly between the level-5 'fix the case and move on' and level-8 'propagate the corrected model' anchors, i.e. a 7.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that emulates the Stripe REST API at the wire level, faithful enough that the real `stripe` Python SDK works unchanged. Difficulty comes from breadth (12+ resource families, list/error envelopes, restricted keys) AND depth on three explicitly named traps with subtle concurrency/temporal semantics (idempotency replay incl. cached errors and same-key serialization, webhook retry/backoff/re-signing, PaymentIntent state machine), all offline against an external contract the agent must reconstruct. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep research of the real Stripe contract, milestone decomposition across a large surface, SDK-driven verification, progress tracking, and course-correction when compatibility breaks.

dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment
dimensions.description: Understanding the externally-defined Stripe wire contract (resource shapes, error codes, test PANs, list/idempotency/webhook semantics) and the SDK's expectations before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is really the real Stripe API; fidelity is graded against SDK behavior the agent must infer, not against this prose. Guessing field names, error codes, or the test-PAN set produces silently non-compliant output.

anchors.0: Starts coding straight from the prompt; invents field names, error codes, and PANs with no reference to actual Stripe behavior.
anchors.3: Recalls a few Stripe shapes from memory; covers the obvious resources but leaves error envelope, list envelope, or PAN set half-guessed.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error `{type,code,...}` mapping, list envelope, the published test-PAN set — and confirms how the SDK sets `api_base`/auth headers before building on them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract for the hard parts too: idempotency key scope `(api_key, key, body)`, webhook signature format, PaymentIntent status transitions, restricted-key scopes — grounded in how the real API/SDK behaves, and revisits sources as gaps surface mid-build.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-correcting reconstruction: cross-checks each subsystem's behavior against concrete SDK round-trips or documented Stripe semantics, catches under-specified corners (decline_code vs code, replay of cached error bodies, re-signing for replay windows) early, and lets findings reshape the design rather than discovering mismatches late.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered hierarchy — auth/boot skeleton, CRUD resources, then the risk-heavy idempotency/webhook/state-machine subsystems — each with a clear done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is too large to hold in one push, and the three named traps carry most of the risk; a flat, breadth-first slog will run out of horizon before the hard semantics are correct.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between endpoints ad hoc with no ordering or done-conditions.
anchors.3: A flat endpoint checklist with no risk prioritization and no explicit 'done' criteria per item.
anchors.5: Clear milestones (boot+auth first, then resource groups, then the traps) with rough done-conditions, and recognizes the three traps as distinct workstreams.
anchors.8: Risk-aware sequencing: gets a bootable auth'd skeleton verifiable early, then deliberately front-loads or ring-fences the high-risk subsystems (idempotency serialization, webhook backoff/re-sign, PI state machine) as first-class milestones each with an explicit check, rather than burying them in CRUD.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that visibly de-risks the whole horizon: dependencies made explicit (e.g. PaymentIntent charges before refunds before subscription invoices), the trickiest semantics scheduled while budget remains, and the plan carries concrete acceptance conditions per milestone that later verification maps onto.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how correctness is confirmed — exercising routes with the real `stripe` SDK / requests, and building targeted checks for idempotency, webhook retry, and state-machine edge cases — beyond 'it returns 200'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Wire-level compatibility and the trap semantics fail silently; only active verification (ideally through the SDK the way the verifier will) distinguishes a plausible-looking response from a compliant one.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because the code was written.
anchors.3: Manual curl of a couple of happy paths; no SDK check, no coverage of error bodies or the trap behaviors.
anchors.5: Boots the service, smoke-tests health and several CRUD flows, and checks a few error/edge cases — but leaves the hardest semantics (concurrent idempotent retries, webhook backoff, illegal state transitions) largely unverified.
anchors.8: Verifies through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and constructs specific checks for the traps: replaying an idempotency key (incl. a cached error body), same-key-different-body → 400, capturing a succeeded intent → 400, invalid PAN → decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff.
anchors.10: A deliberate verification harness that covers happy paths, error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, list pagination, restricted-key 403s, and the concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charge, re-signed late webhook deliveries), re-run after changes so regressions are caught rather than assumed away.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture over 12+ resource families and the trap subsystems, and detecting when effort is stuck or circling on one behavior.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing customers while subscriptions/invoices/webhooks remain unstarted, or re-debugging the same idempotency case repeatedly.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; forgets whole resource families or repeats work.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; discovers late that major endpoints or the webhook worker were never implemented.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and their status, and generally knows what remains.
anchors.8: Actively maintains coverage against the full route table, notices when stuck on one behavior and time-boxes it, and reallocates attention so no major area is silently dropped.
anchors.10: Continuous, accurate accounting across the whole horizon: distinguishes implemented-and-verified from implemented-only from missing, catches thrashing/circular debugging early and names it, and adjusts pace to land the full surface plus the traps within budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when SDK round-trips, error shapes, or trap semantics diverge from expectations — rather than pressing on with a falsified assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reconstructing an external contract guarantees wrong initial assumptions (field names, signature scheme, state rules); the agent must let contradicting evidence rewrite the design, sometimes structurally (e.g. how idempotency serialization or the billing worker is built).

anchors.0: Ignores failing SDK calls or wrong outputs; keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Patches surface symptoms (tweaks a field) without revisiting the underlying wrong model, so the same class of mismatch recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the root cause for that case and moves on.
anchors.8: Treats divergences as signals about the contract: on discovering e.g. a wrong signature format or state-transition rule, updates the mental model and propagates the fix across related endpoints, not just the one that failed.
anchors.10: Fluid, evidence-driven correction across the horizon, including structural pivots when needed (rethinking idempotency locking, webhook re-signing, or state-machine modeling once reality contradicts the plan), while preserving already-verified work — never barrels ahead on a falsified assumption.
